title: Ads Are Machine Learning 1.0: How AppLovin Earned an 84% Margin From It
dek: Advertising isn't AI's past tense — it's the earliest and most profitable deployment of deep learning. AppLovin used recommendation models to build an 84% EBITDA margin in the $50 billion mobile game ad market, and became its own best investor with $6 billion of buybacks.
why: A CEO who almost never gives interviews explains the shared technical roots of advertising and AI, the buyback playbook through a 92% drawdown, and why a Chinese engineering team is an advantage. High information density, worth listening to.
who: Founders, investors and engineers watching ad tech, recommendation systems and AI commercialization; anyone who wants to know how a small team builds a moat in a field full of giants.
skip: If ad tech details don't interest you, the part from 8:07 to 9:07 about whether phones eavesdrop can be skipped.

points.h: Mobile game advertising is a $50 billion market
points.body: Adam says outsiders underestimate the scale of mobile gaming: over a billion adults play casual mobile games every day, and these people are household decision-makers. Two years ago AppLovin disclosed $11 billion of annual ad spend on its own platform, and it has grown at roughly 60% year over year since, which by rough math puts it at about $20 billion today. But that isn't the whole market — many other ad companies monetize in this ecosystem, so double that number and the entire mobile game ecosystem spends roughly $50 billion a year on advertising. He notes that not long ago social was also just a $50 billion opportunity.

points.h: Advertising is machine learning's earliest and most profitable implementation
points.body: Adam calls advertising ML 1.0: it was the first deployment of all these technologies that now drive AI. Large language models create more economic value today than advertising, but advertising is an extremely profitable implementation of deep learning models. Recommendation systems and large language models have different architectures, but their trajectories are highly similar — research in large language models can transfer to recommendation systems and vice versa; many large language model researchers spent the early part of their careers looking at ad systems. The beauty of the ad business is that you build a model to predict a future outcome, and the value of that prediction can be converted into money immediately.

points.h: Search ads create no economic increment; discovery ads do
points.body: Adam splits advertising into two categories. One is bottom-of-funnel advertising: the consumer already knows what they want to buy and is just doing research to complete the transaction — that's Google Search's business, and large language models will compete with Google Search almost entirely in that area. The other is his own field: not knowing user intent, creating a demand that didn't previously exist, so the user sees it and thinks ‘this looks really cool, I want to buy it right now’. He stresses that the transaction in search or in a large language model was going to happen anyway, so there isn't much economic expansion there; discovery advertising creates economic increment, which is why Meta's ad business is so strong and what AppLovin wants to do.

points.h: Your phone isn't listening, but your behavior is tracked
points.body: Faced with the question of ‘I talk about something at lunch and then an ad for it appears’, Adam says it's more likely you did something trackable earlier — a search, a website visit, a product search — without realizing it, and then you said something related and started seeing related ads. He states plainly that AppLovin does not track location at all, arguing that tracking precise location to render ads is a very heavy concept, and that the data transfer required to parse microphone content in real time and translate it into an ad is unrealistic. But he concedes that if you're on a social network, relationship data between you and others can of course drive the ad experience — for example, a friend searched for something and you might see a related ad, which he doesn't see as a problem.

points.h: From $28 billion to $3.8 billion, then it started buying itself
points.body: AppLovin went public in April 2021 with $600 million of EBITDA at a market cap of about $28 billion, peaking at $40 billion. In 2022 the stock fell almost every day, down to a market cap of about $3.8 billion — in a year when the company did $1 billion of EBITDA. Adam's read: market cap is determined by the quality of investors, and at the time a lot of companies were going public at the same time, blue-chip investors hadn't done the research to figure out what this company with the silly name was, and the result was no demand and lots of supply, with the valuation falling from 50x EBITDA to under 4x. His response was to stop talking to investors and instead use the large amounts of cash the company generated to buy back aggressively, eventually buying about $6 billion of its own stock and retiring 20% to 25% of the shares outstanding.

points.h: When the stock fell 92%, family called to ask if you wanted to kill yourself
points.body: Adam says that period was hard, that family and friends would call to ask if he wanted to kill himself, and his answer was that the stock was still at $10 and had still gone up a lot. But the truly hard part was realizing that as CEO, his team was getting the same calls, and they didn't have his composure or his equity. So they rallied the team around a ‘we versus the world’ mentality, and extended a performance stock program usually reserved for the CEO to key people across the company, telling them: it's hard right now, the house you thought you had is gone, but if you hold on and recover, the upside is huge. Later investors started coming back, the company switched from regression models to deep learning models, the ad algorithm got better, advertiser returns got better, and the business started growing fast.

points.h: A week in New York took the market cap from $28 billion to $55 billion
points.body: When the new model launched in April 2023 the company still wasn't talking to investors, so the outside world didn't know. By around September 2023 the stock was at $80 with good results, and Adam judged the market cap high enough that it couldn't buy back that aggressively anymore, so he went to New York and started talking to investors. In that one week the stock went from $80 to $150, and the market cap from $28 billion to $55 billion — just because he went out and said ‘our company is still here, we survived’. He describes sitting in meetings and being able to read the person across the table texting a friend to buy. Over the next two and a half years the stock went from $9 to $750, a $250 billion market cap. His conclusion is that public market investors and private investors aren't that different, both chase trends, just often later than you'd like.

points.h: After privacy rules tightened, users complained ads got worse
points.body: Adam says in these areas you want regulatory clarity, and once the rules are clear, technology can respond. Five years ago you could target users precisely on iOS; today if users say no precise targeting, you can only bundle them into groups and serve worse ads. The interesting result of this change is that after Apple's change the company received a flood of user complaints saying ‘show me more relevant ads, you're showing me a bunch of junk now’. So he offers a duality: on one hand you need privacy regulation so tech companies know what to do, on the other hand consumers do want relevant ads — when you watch a 30-second ad in a game to get an extra life, you're getting something with monetary value, and you don't want to spend those 30 seconds on junk.

points.h: It bought game studios for training data, then sold them off
points.body: Adam explains the motive for buying game studios was data: building the first deep learning model requires data, and game studios are usually unwilling to share data with a third-party company, so they bought their own studios, fed the training data into the first model, built a model that was very successful in the market and started growing fast. Once it worked, third parties started coming to them proactively, and they divested and sold those game businesses. This clarifies outside speculation about whether AppLovin was becoming a game publisher — what it bought was data, not long-term game assets.

points.h: The typical shopper isn't the person on Twitter chasing new tech
points.body: On agents and agentic commerce, Adam thinks one part of the world will use agents to optimize fixed shopping behaviors, like handing a supplement subscription to an agent to optimize monthly and deliver on time. But discovery platforms don't work that way, and the typical shopper isn't the kind of person who uses agents deeply and lives on Twitter chasing the latest tech. He says his audience is ‘the New York Times audience’, and plenty of people still use Yahoo products today. The typical shopper wants to find products, wants to browse, wants to complete the transaction flow, wants to compare prices, wants to track shipping; even if you tell them afterward an agent could have saved 20%, on a $50 transaction it doesn't matter, because the dopamine of going through the flow is what they enjoy. He thinks the industry over-indexes on the Twitter bubble and forgets the ordinary shopper isn't like that.

points.h: Every morning you wake up feeling you're about to be killed, so you run faster
points.body: Faced with the question of how a small company wins when Meta and Alphabet have the best engineers and have done advertising for decades, Adam says one thing that got them here is that they never think they've won, they wake up every day feeling they're about to be killed, so they have to work harder. The company stays lean and has gathered a lot of domain experts truly focused on the mobile game experience and on converting it into transaction behavior. He believes that if you're very focused and stay lean, you can run faster than the giants, and that gives you the ability to challenge them.

points.h: An 84% EBITDA margin that no one can compete away
points.body: Adam says AppLovin's EBITDA margin is the best in the market at 84%, so he doesn't think there's much leakage. He explains the business model: advertisers come in with a transaction model, say selling lipstick, and the company gives them an arbitrage — they buy consumers from AppLovin, and when the consumer completes the transaction it immediately covers the acquisition cost. The consumer spends $20 on lipstick, the advertiser pays AppLovin less than $20 minus cost of goods sold, the advertiser is happy and spends more, and this performance model is very scalable. The company isn't the whole chain, isn't the advertiser itself, but empowers advertisers to reach consumers, while operating extremely lean and being extremely algorithm- and automation-driven, so there aren't many leakage points. To the argument that an 85% EBIT margin means you might be over-earning and competitors would be willing to take 60% or 50% to grab share, Adam's response is: these technologies are very complex, and if you can innovate and have differentiated data, you can build an advantage — just as Anthropic shouldn't have run away with the language model field, but once a model reaches scale and is adopted by a large community, it becomes a moat others struggle to cross.

points.h: A Chinese team is an advantage; I'm often the dumbest person in the room
points.body: On Chinese teams, Adam says Chinese people are very humble, very hardworking, very sharp, and whether in China, the US or anywhere else in the world, working with them is working with the smartest people in the world. One of his goals when starting a company was to work with excellent people and figure things out together. He says when he sits in a room with some of the people on his team, he knows he's very likely the dumbest person in that room, and that makes him excited to come to work.
